title: I went to LA's $333 dinner party to dine with ghostly spirits — what I actually found stunned me more
excerpt: There are few things Angelenos love more than a fancy dinner and a brush with the supernatural, and this evening promised both.
content:
It was a little like kindergarten.

In a single file line, 24 fully grown adults calmly marched up the stairs and into the attic, taking off our shoes and finding a spot to sit in the dimly lit room.

There are few things Angelenos love more than a fancy dinner and a brush with the supernatural, and this evening promised both.

Spirits were high when guests arrived at Kristina Robbins’ Craftsman-style West Adams home on a cool November night for her “Memento Mori” dinner party, the latest edition of the Sweet Antelope supper club.

The swanky dinner, where “Angel Tickets” cost $333 a pop, promised attendees a chance to connect with spirits from the other side, in addition to a multi-course meal. No refunds were issued for guests who didn’t meet their maker.

Guests were encouraged to bring a photo with them to create an “altar” on the dinner tables. Most seemed to bring photos of deceased relatives, while some brought photos of their younger selves, or of happy memories with loved ones.

The evening began just after 5 p.m. in the backyard, where guests mingled and munched on hors d’oeuvres including a 5-spice duck crostini and grilled gorgonzola mushrooms. A specialty cocktail was served at a bar manned by Robbins’ 20-something son Finlay.

Robbins, a documentary filmmaker, began Sweet Antelope Supper Club in 2023 after noticing that the art of dinner parties was being lost.

“The act of inviting strangers into your home is kind of a sacred thing,” says Robbins. Almost all of the food served at her dinners is grown in her backyard garden. The rest is sourced from local farmers.

Robbins’ passion for entertaining has now grown into a full-blown business. As part of the Sweet Antelope Supper Club, she regularly hosts storytelling dinner parties where conversation is sparked after guests hear from a professional storyteller. She also rents out her picturesque three-story home for corporate team dinners and private events.

“I’ve always been the person who brought people together. I love to cook. I love to have people over for dinner,” Robbins says.

Tonight’s theme, “Memento Mori,” is meant to remind guests to “live fiercely, take risks, say the thing, and stop saving the good stuff for someday,” was the first of its kind.

While I admit I’m not super sentimental about death, and am generally skeptical of pretty much any kind of supernatural encounter, I came with an open mind, anxiously hoping to come in contact with the other side, or at least make a friend or two.

During the cocktail hour, each guest was given a small piece of wood inscribed with their name, and asked to burn it over a fire to “release” things holding us back.

Then it was time for the ritual to begin. We headed up to the attic, where medium Aja Daashuur led the group on a “journey through the veil.” While adequately relaxing, the journey felt like more of a guided meditation than a spiritual experience.

We were asked to imagine various scents and sounds, and then acquainted with our “spirit guide” for the evening. Maybe it was because I was hungry, but I couldn’t envision a thing. If I listened closely, I probably could’ve heard a few people sleeping.

After what felt like a lifetime, but was probably around half an hour, we opened our eyes and were walked back downstairs to begin dinner. The evening’s “spirit-led” seating meant that people who came with guests were likely split between the dinner’s three tables, making for an eclectic mix of strangers.

Tables were decorated with flowers, candles, and personalized place settings including a leaf with each guest’s name written on it, and cards detailing your “spirit archetype.”

Here’s where they lost me. Each guest received two cards with two different archetypes.

One main archetype, and one archetype that was ‘in conversation’ with your main archetype. If this sounds convoluted, that’s because it was.

My main archetype was “The Reformer.” As an out-of-the-box thinker often keen to see things differently, the title suited me. It felt good to get a guide that made sense with my personality, but wasn’t exactly a spiritual awakening.

Thankfully, the lack of clarity about spirit guides did not stop the flow of conversation. As the first course was served, a delicious pumpkin locro stew — served inside of an actual pumpkin — the table came alive.

We soon realized we shared innumerable connections. Two of us had recently lost dogs, both 18 years old, just days apart. One of us frequently bought the snow cones that the other sells at a local market, and three of us were Sagittarians.

By the time the main course, a flatiron steak (or a cauliflower tatin for vegans) was served, my little table of seven had become family.

Daashuur stopped by each of the tables several times throughout the dinner to see if we had any questions about our spirit guides. No one asked anything, probably because we wouldn’t know where to begin, or because we were simply enjoying conversation too much.

As special as it felt, Robbins says most of her guests walk away with the same feeling.

“Oftentimes people will come up to me and tell me about all these weird connections everybody had,” said Robbins.

“If we’re given the structure that allows us to probe in a way that we don’t normally get to, then you find those things.”

After dinner, the evening was capped by dessert in the backyard. A sweet passionfruit pavlova topped with mixed berries and raspberry dust was served, along with piping hot tea.

As I spoke with a tablemate who I’d gotten close with throughout the night, I realized it’d be time to leave soon. There were no visions of dead ancestors or glimpses into the future, but I did meet a diverse group of new people who bonded over their experiences in loss and life.

I left the dinner about as skeptical about mediums as the next person, but I also got to eat some delicious food, and gulp down several glasses of wine — all included in the price tag.

While my spirit guide didn’t quite materialize, the human connection at the table was priceless.
